front: What causes over half of truck driver crash deaths?
back: Rollovers.
why: A high, heavy load tips more easily.

front: A full rig rolls over how many times more than an empty one?
back: 10 times.
why: More cargo makes the center of gravity higher.

front: What 2 things help stop rollovers?
back: Keep cargo low. Go slow in turns.

front: What can a fast lane change do to a trailer?
back: Flip it over.
why: This is the crack-the-whip effect.

front: What causes the crack-the-whip effect?
back: Rearward amplification.

front: Rearward amplification of 2.0 means what?
back: Rear trailer is 2 times as likely to tip.
why: It is compared to the tractor.

front: Triples: the last trailer tips how many times easier than the tractor?
back: 3.5 times.
why: This number is the rearward amplification.

front: In a sudden turn with doubles, which trailer tips first?
back: The rear trailer.
why: The whip is strongest at the tail.

front: How should you steer when pulling trailers?
back: Gently and smoothly.
why: A quick jerk of the wheel can tip the trailer.

front: Which takes longer to stop: an empty rig or a loaded one?
back: The empty rig.
why: Stiff springs give poor grip, so wheels lock.

front: Does a bobtail stop faster than a full rig?
back: No. It takes longer to stop.

front: Which trailers can get stuck on raised rail crossings?
back: Low ones: lowboy, car carrier, moving van.
why: Possum-belly livestock trailers too.

front: What tractor setup can hang up on a rail crossing?
back: Single-axle tractor, landing gear set for tandem.
why: The long trailer sits too low in the middle.

front: You are stuck on the tracks. What do you do first?
back: Get out and away from the tracks.

front: After leaving a stuck rig on tracks, who do you call?
back: 911 or the number posted at the crossing.
why: Give the crossing DOT number if posted.

front: What happens when trailer wheels lock up?
back: The trailer swings out. A trailer jackknife.

front: When is a trailer jackknife most likely?
back: When the trailer is empty or light.

front: What is the best way to spot a trailer skid?
back: Look in your mirrors.
why: Check mirrors any time you brake hard.

front: How do you stop a trailer skid?
back: Let off the brakes.
why: Rolling wheels grip the road again.

front: Should you use the trailer hand brake to fix a skid?
back: No.
why: Trailer brakes caused the skid.

front: What is offtracking?
back: Rear wheels take a tighter path than front wheels.
why: It is also called cheating.

front: Which wheels offtrack the most?
back: Rear wheels of the last trailer.
why: Longer rigs offtrack more.

front: Why keep your rear close to the curb in a turn?
back: So cars cannot pass you on the right.

front: If you must use another lane to turn, when do you swing wide?
back: As you finish the turn.
why: Not before you start the turn.

front: Backing a trailer, which way do you turn the wheel?
back: Opposite the way you want to go.

front: If you must back on a curve, back to which side?
back: The driver's side.
why: So you can see.

front: What should you use the trailer hand valve for?
back: Only to test trailer brakes.

front: Why not use the trailer hand valve while driving?
back: It can make the trailer skid.
why: The foot brake is safer. It brakes all wheels.

front: Can you park using the trailer hand valve?
back: Never.
why: Air can leak out and free the brakes.

front: What does the tractor protection valve do?
back: Keeps tractor air if the trailer leaks or breaks away.

front: At what air pressure does the tractor protection valve close?
back: 20 to 45 psi.

front: When the tractor protection valve closes, what happens to the trailer?
back: Its emergency brakes come on.

front: What does the trailer air supply control look like?
back: A red 8-sided knob.
why: Shaped like a stop sign.

front: What happens when you push in the trailer air supply knob?
back: Air goes to the trailer.

front: What happens when you pull out the trailer air supply knob?
back: Air shuts off. Trailer emergency brakes come on.

front: How many air lines run between each unit?
back: 2: service and emergency.

front: What controls air in the service line?
back: The foot brake or trailer hand valve.
why: It carries brake air to the trailer brakes.

front: What is another name for the emergency line?
back: Supply line.

front: What are the 2 jobs of the emergency line?
back: Fills trailer air tanks. Controls emergency brakes.

front: What happens if the emergency line breaks or loses air?
back: Trailer emergency brakes come on.
why: The air supply knob also pops out.

front: What color is the emergency line? The service line?
back: Emergency is red. Service is blue.
why: Red for emergency, like a fire truck.

front: What are glad hands?
back: Couplers that join tractor and trailer air lines.

front: At what angle do you join glad hands?
back: 90 degrees, then turn to lock.

front: You crossed the air lines. What happens to trailer spring brakes?
back: They stay on.
why: Supply air goes to the wrong line.

front: Crossed lines on an old trailer with no spring brakes. The risk?
back: You could drive with no trailer brakes.

front: What are dummy couplers for?
back: Keep dirt and water out of unused lines.

front: How often should you drain trailer air tanks?
back: Every day.
why: Water and oil can make brakes fail.

front: What is another name for shut-off valves?
back: Cut-out cocks.

front: Which shut-off valves should be closed?
back: Only the ones at the back of the last trailer.
why: All others stay open.

front: Why chock a trailer with no spring brakes when parked?
back: Tank air leaks away. Then it has no brakes.

front: Trailers built on or after what date need ABS?
back: March 1, 1998.

front: Where is the trailer ABS warning lamp?
back: Left side. It is yellow.

front: Why keep the fifth wheel plate greased?
back: So friction does not cause steering trouble.

front: How should the fifth wheel sit before coupling?
back: Tilted down to the rear. Jaws open.

front: Before coupling, a sliding fifth wheel must be what?
back: Locked.

front: Before you back under, how is the trailer held still?
back: Wheels chocked or spring brakes on.

front: Why never back under a trailer at an angle?
back: You could push it sideways and break the landing gear.

front: How high should the trailer be for coupling?
back: Low enough that the tractor lifts it a bit.
why: Too low hits the nose. Too high may not lock.

front: Which air line do you hook up first?
back: Emergency line, then service line.

front: After supplying air, why shut the engine off?
back: So you can hear the trailer brakes work.

front: Before backing under the trailer, what do you do to its brakes?
back: Lock them. Pull out the air supply knob.

front: How do you do the tug test?
back: Pull forward gently with trailer brakes locked.
why: Raise the landing gear a little first.

front: Why take the key before checking the coupling?
back: So no one moves the truck while you're under it.

front: How much gap between upper and lower fifth wheel?
back: None.

front: What does a gap between the fifth wheel plates mean?
back: Kingpin may be on top of the jaws.
why: The trailer could come loose easily.

front: The locking jaws should close around which part of the kingpin?
back: The shank, not the head.

front: How far do you raise the landing gear to drive?
back: All the way up.
why: Not just off the ground. Part way up can catch on tracks.

front: After raising landing gear, what 2 gaps do you check?
back: Tractor frame to landing gear. Tires to trailer nose.

front: What is the last step of coupling?
back: Remove and store the wheel chocks.

front: How do you ease pressure on the locking jaws?
back: Back up gently, then set the parking brake.

front: When should you chock trailer wheels before uncoupling?
back: If no spring brakes, or if unsure.

front: Loaded trailer: what do you do after landing gear touches ground?
back: Crank a few more turns in low gear.
why: Do not lift the trailer off the fifth wheel.

front: When you first pull out, where do you stop the tractor?
back: With tractor frame still under the trailer.
why: It catches the trailer if landing gear fails.

front: What if the fifth wheel is set too far forward?
back: Frame may hit landing gear. Cab may hit trailer.
why: This happens in turns.

front: How do you check that air reaches all trailers?
back: Open rear shut-off valves on last trailer. Listen for air.

front: How do you test the tractor protection valve?
back: Engine off. Pump the brake pedal. Knob should pop out.
why: It should pop out at 20 to 45 psi.

front: How do you test trailer emergency brakes?
back: Pull the air supply knob. Tug gently. Trailer should hold.

front: How do you test trailer service brakes?
back: Roll slowly. Apply the hand valve. Feel brakes grab.

front: Where are shut-off valves found?
back: At the back of trailers that tow other trailers.
why: They are in the service and emergency lines.

front: Trailer is too high when coupling. What can happen?
back: It may not couple right.
why: Too low, and the tractor can hit the trailer nose.

front: Should you look into the back of the fifth wheel?
back: Yes. Check the jaws closed on the kingpin.
why: They must close on the shank, not the head.
